title: Sub-Goal Generation
summary: Decompose broad objectives into bounded sub-goals with explicit dependencies, measurable completion criteria, and a controlled expansion budget.
overview: Sub-goal generation translates a high-level objective into smaller outcomes that can be independently attempted and verified. A useful sub-goal describes a result, required evidence, constraints, and its relationship to the parent objective. It is not simply a list of verbs or a longer restatement of the original request.

The architecture must prevent decomposition from expanding scope indefinitely. Track a goal tree or dependency graph, inherit authorization and budgets, and reject children that do not contribute to parent acceptance. Some objectives cannot be decomposed cleanly because intermediate choices change the problem; those require explicit replanning rather than pretending the first tree is complete.

production.poc: A prototype can ask a model for a short goal list and have a person mark useful versus redundant entries. Evaluate coverage and executability before measuring fluency.
production.production: Production validates each sub-goal against available capabilities, required inputs, and completion tests. Give every child a stable identity and explicit owner.
production.scale: At enterprise scale, limit branching and depth, detect duplicate goals semantically and structurally, and aggregate progress by business value. Ten completed trivial children do not imply that the decisive parent requirement is nearly finished.

components.name: Goal decomposer
components.role: Proposes child outcomes and explains their contribution to parent completion.

components.name: Capability matcher
components.role: Checks that each child can be executed with available tools and permissions.

components.name: Goal graph
components.role: Stores dependencies, ownership, status, and inherited constraints for each child.

components.name: Completion evaluator
components.role: Verifies child artifacts against defined acceptance criteria.

components.name: Expansion controller
components.role: Caps depth, branching, aggregate cost, and repeated decomposition attempts.

flow.title: Define parent outcome
flow.description: Capture the intended deliverable and distinguish mandatory requirements from optional improvements.

flow.title: Propose children
flow.description: Generate bounded outcomes with evidence needs and explicit dependencies.

flow.title: Validate coverage
flow.description: Check for missing requirements, duplicate work, impossible capabilities, and scope expansion.

flow.title: Assign execution
flow.description: Map valid children to workers and allocate budgets while reserving integration capacity.

flow.title: Evaluate artifacts
flow.description: Accept sub-goal completion only when its evidence and output contract are satisfied.

flow.title: Aggregate meaningfully
flow.description: Determine parent completion from required outcomes, and replan only unresolved portions.

useCase.title: Preparing a product recall response
useCase.situation: A food producer receives a contamination alert that may affect several production lots and distribution partners.
useCase.problem: The request to prepare a recall response is too broad for one reliable tool sequence and can omit downstream shipment analysis.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must identify affected material, trace distribution, and prepare evidence-backed communication drafts for authorized review.
useCase.architecture: A decomposer creates lot-identification, shipment-tracing, and notice-preparation goals with dependencies and controlled access to traceability systems.
runtime: The first child establishes verified lot boundaries; shipment tracing consumes those identifiers rather than guessing from product descriptions.
Notice drafting begins only when destination evidence is available, and parent acceptance requires all mandatory traceability gaps to be visible.
useCase.failure: If a distributor feed is incomplete, its child remains unresolved and the final package highlights the missing coverage for the response team.
useCase.impact: Measure requirement coverage, duplicate child work, unexecutable goals, and unresolved critical dependencies. Drafting many notices is not equivalent to completing traceability.

tradeoffs.benefit: Work can be delegated and verified independently.
tradeoffs.cost: Excessive granularity increases coordination and storage overhead.

tradeoffs.benefit: Unusual objectives can be adapted to available evidence.
tradeoffs.cost: Goal quality varies and requires validation.
Some tasks remain blocked while uncertain upstream work is resolved.

failures.scenario: A child broadens the original authority
failures.detection: Constraint checks identify a proposed action outside the parent scope.
failures.recovery: Reject that child and regenerate within allowed boundaries.

failures.scenario: Two children request the same expensive analysis
failures.detection: Goal fingerprints and input references overlap.
failures.recovery: Merge equivalent work and share the validated artifact.

mistakes.fix: Require an observable result and completion test.

mistakes.mistake: Counting completed children as equal progress
mistakes.fix: Weight mandatory parent requirements and critical dependencies.
Reserve ownership and budget for assembling the final deliverable.

whenToUse: Different capabilities can execute independent parts.
Coverage of mandatory requirements matters more than conversational fluency.
whenNotToUse: A single bounded operation already completes the objective.
Intermediate outcomes cannot be validated or assigned.
The decomposition overhead exceeds the task's useful work.
checklist: Require completion tests for each child.
